## Overview

The Koryaks are an Indigenous people of the Russian Far East living immediately north of the Kamchatka Peninsula, in Kamchatka Krai and along the coastlands of the Bering Sea. Their cultural borders include Tigilsk in the south and the Anadyr basin in the north. The Koryaks are divided broadly into coastal Nemelan, or Nymylan, “village dwellers,” whose livelihoods include fishing and marine mammal hunting, and inland Chaucu, or Chauchuven, “rich in reindeer,” who follow reindeer herds as they graze with the seasons. Their language and Alutor are linguistically close to Chukchi, and these languages belong to the Chukotko-Kamchatkan language family. According to the 2010 census, 7,953 Koryaks lived in Russia.

## Material culture

### Clothing & dress

Koryak clothing was made from reindeer hides. Men wore baggy pants, a hide shirt often fitted with a hood, boots, and traditional caps made of reindeer skin. Women wore similar clothing, but their shirts were longer and reached the calves. The sources state that men and women nowadays often replace hide clothing with cloth, although reindeer-skin boots and caps remain in use. Women often wear a head cloth and skirt, while using a reindeer-skin robe in cold weather.

### Architecture

The Koryaks lived in domed tents called *jajanga*, or *yaranga*, a name derived from the Chukchi term. These dwellings were similar to a tipi of the American Plains Indians but less vertical. Their framework was covered with many reindeer skins. The centre contained a hearth, later replaced by an iron stove, and reindeer-hide beds were placed to the east in the *chum*. Small cupboards stored family food, clothing, and personal items. Some Koryaks lived in yurts. Few families still use the *yaranga* as a dwelling, although some use it during trips to the tundra.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They do describe tools and weapons made from reindeer body parts, as well as small cupboards used for storing food, clothing, and personal items. Snowshoes were made by lashing reindeer sinew and hide strips to a tennis-racket-shaped hoop of birch bark or willow.

## Music & performance

 They state that Koryak mythology centres on the supernatural shaman Quikil, or Big-Raven, who was created by the Supreme Being as the first man and protector of the Koryak.

## Festivals & rituals

 They describe a religious world in which the Supreme Being resides in Heaven with his family and may punish immoral acts by falling asleep, leaving people vulnerable to unsuccessful hunting and other ills. The sources also identify Quikil, or Big-Raven, as a supernatural shaman and protector of the Koryak.

## Foodways

Interior Koryak life revolved around reindeer, the main source of food. The people used all parts of the animal for sewing materials, clothing, tools, and weapons. Reindeer meat was mostly eaten roasted, while blood, marrow, and milk were drunk or eaten raw. Liver, heart, kidneys, and tongue were considered delicacies. Salmon and other freshwater fish, together with berries and roots, were important because reindeer flesh lacked some vitamins and minerals and did not provide necessary dietary fibre. Coastal Koryaks primarily relied on hunting whales and other marine mammals for food. Today, Koryaks also buy processed foods such as bread, cereal, and canned fish. They sell some reindeer each year for money and can increase their herds because of the large reindeer population.

## Oral tradition & literature

Koryak mythology centres on Quikil, or Big-Raven, a supernatural shaman created by the Supreme Being as the first man and protector of the Koryak. Big Raven myths are also found in Southeast Alaska among the Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian, and other Native people of the Pacific Northwest Coast Amerindians.

## Language & religion

Koryak and Alutor, which is often regarded as a dialect of Koryak, are linguistically close to Chukchi. Koryak, Alutor, and Chukchi belong to the Chukotko-Kamchatkan language family. The Koryaks are more distantly related linguistically to the Itelmens of the Kamchatka Peninsula. The sources name several terms for the Supreme Being: *ŋajŋənen*, “Universe/World”; *ineɣitelʔən*, “Supervisor”; *ɣət͡ɕɣoletənvəlʔən*, “Master-of-the-Upper-World”; and *ɣət͡ɕɣolʔən*, “One-on-High.”
